summary.text: Gymnosperms are woody, perennial plants that make seeds without a protective outer covering, and the group includes conifers, cycads, ginkgos and gnetophytes.
The name means naked seed, because the seeds are not enclosed in an ovary the way those of flowering plants are.
Conifers are by far the most abundant living gymnosperms, in a group of over 1,000 living species.

items.prompt: A pine seed sits in the open on a cone scale, while a cherry seed is wrapped in fruit. Which fact about gymnosperms explains the pine?

options.label: They cannot make seeds at all, only spores
Their cones are fruits with the seeds inside the flesh
Their ovules and seeds are not enclosed in an ovary
Their seeds form underground and are pushed up later

items.explain: Gymnosperm seeds are unenclosed, in contrast to flowering plants, whose seeds and ovules sit inside an ovary.

items.prompt: A forester looks at a mature cone-bearing tree. Which phase of the life cycle is that tree?

options.label: The diploid sporophyte, while the gamete-bearing phase is short-lived
The haploid gametophyte, with a short-lived sporophyte
An equal mix of both phases
A gametophyte that lives on the sporophyte permanently

items.explain: Gymnosperms have a sporophyte-dominant life cycle: most of their life is spent with diploid cells, and the gametophyte is short-lived.

items.prompt: A homeowner has a single pine and asks whether it is one of separate male and female trees. What is true of almost all conifers?

options.label: They need a second tree of the other sex to form any cones
They carry male and female cones on the same tree
They switch sex each year
They bear only male cones until old age

items.explain: Conifers are almost all monoecious, with male and female cones on the same tree, unlike the 65 percent of gymnosperms that are dioecious.

items.prompt: A park ranger points to a ginkgo and says its group has no living near relatives. What does she mean?

options.label: Ginkgos are extinct and survive only as fossils
Ginkgos are a branch of the conifers with hundreds of species
Ginkgos are the only gymnosperms with flowers
Ginkgo biloba is the single living species of its group

items.explain: Of the extant gymnosperm groups, Ginkgo has just one species.

items.prompt: A traveler wants to see wild cycads, small palm-like trees. Where should she head?

options.label: Tropical regions near the equator
Frozen northern forests
Cool alpine meadows
High dry mountain deserts

items.explain: A majority of cycads are native to tropical climates and are most abundant in regions near the equator.

items.prompt: A cycad grows in poor soil. What helps it get nitrogen?

options.label: Insects trapped by its leaves and digested
Nitrogen stored in its seeds from last year
Small specialised roots that host nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria
A swollen taproot that absorbs it from deep rock

items.explain: Cycas has small specialised coralloid roots associated with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria.

paragraphs.heading: Naked seeds
paragraphs.text: Gymnosperms are woody seed plants that live for many years, and they include conifers, cycads, ginkgos and gnetophytes. Their name comes from Greek words meaning naked seed. Their seeds, called ovules before fertilisation, are not wrapped inside an ovary the way the seeds of flowering plants are. Instead the seeds grow on the face of scales or leaves, often reshaped into cones, or they sit on their own, as in yew and Ginkgo.

paragraphs.heading: The living groups
paragraphs.text: More than 1,000 species of gymnosperm are alive today. Conifers, meaning pines, cypresses and their relatives, are by far the biggest group, with about 600 to 630 species. Next come the cycads, small trees that look like palms, with roughly 338 species, most of them native to tropical climates near the equator. The gnetophytes number 95 to 100 species and include Welwitschia, which grows horizontally. Ginkgo biloba, a tall tree with two-lobed leaves, is the only living ginkgo.

paragraphs.heading: How they live
paragraphs.text: Every gymnosperm is a perennial woody plant. They fill fewer ecological roles than flowering plants, yet the group still includes a parasite, Parasitaxus, and a water-dwelling species, Retrophyllum minus. About 65% of gymnosperms have separate male and female plants. Conifers are the exception, since almost all of them carry male and female cones on the same tree, and every conifer is pollinated by the wind.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of spores
paragraphs.text: Like all vascular plants, gymnosperms spend most of their lives in a stage called the sporophyte. The gametophyte, the phase that carries the sex cells, is reduced, short-lived and depends on the sporophyte. Gymnosperms make two types of spore: male microspores form in pollen cones, and female megaspores form in ovulate cones. Microspores mature into pollen grains, which in the end produce sperm cells, while megaspores develop and stay inside the ovule. In pollination, pollen grains are carried from a pollen cone to an ovule.

paragraphs.heading: A deep history
paragraphs.text: Early features of seed plants already show up in fossil progymnosperms from the late Devonian, about 383 million years ago. Scientists once widely held that gymnosperms arose in the Late Carboniferous. Newer evidence from evolutionary family trees points instead to a split from the ancestors of flowering plants in the Early Carboniferous. Their spread into many forms in the late Carboniferous seems to have followed a doubling of their whole genome about 319 million years ago.

paragraphs.heading: Ancient insect partners
paragraphs.text: In the middle of the Mesozoic era, some gymnosperm groups that are now extinct may have been pollinated by scorpionflies, also extinct, whose special mouthparts let them feed on pollination drops. The scorpionflies likely had a give-and-take partnership with gymnosperms, long before nectar-feeding insects evolved alongside flowering plants, and quite separately from them. Other gymnosperms of that time were pollinated by kalligrammatid lacewings.
